files.name: 2026-08-11.md

frontmatter.title: The first commit, and beats become scenes

files.body:
Put the Worldbuilder codebase under version control and immediately tore out the first thing that
wasn't working.

The Story Planner had a beats checklist — tick a box when your story hits a beat. It looked useful
and taught me nothing. A checklist tells you whether something happened; it can't tell you whether
the scene is doing any work. Replaced it with a structured scene-and-sequel model, which asks what
the character wants going in, what stops them, and what they decide as a result. Harder to fill in,
which is the point. A form you can complete without thinking is a form that isn't asking anything.

Also fixed a scene modal you couldn't scroll to the bottom of — a self-inflicted wound, since the
fields I'd just added were the ones out of reach — and made chapters reorderable by dragging.

Starting a log on day one of version control feels like the right moment, even though the app is a
few months old by now. Everything before this exists only as a working directory.

files.name: 2026-08-12.md

frontmatter.title: Search that finds the thing you meant

files.body:
Chapter search in the Manuscript Spine, and a fix for Jots content search that had been matching
titles but not bodies.

Small day. Search is one of those features nobody praises and everybody notices when it's missing, or
worse, when it's there and quietly wrong. A search that returns nothing looks identical to a search
for something that isn't there.

files.name: 2026-08-13.md

frontmatter.title: Scene cards that say how a scene connects

files.body:
Extended the scene card to record three things I'd been keeping in my head: how a scene connects to
the one before it, whether it charges the story positively or negatively, and what kind of
cliffhanger it ends on.

The connector is the one I care about most. A sequence of scenes that are each fine on their own can
still read as a list, and the reason is almost always that nothing in scene four needs scene three
to have happened. Making the connection an explicit field means the gap shows up while I'm planning
rather than on a reread three chapters later.

The rest of the day was making sure those fields don't die in the form. A field you fill in once and
never see again is worse than no field — it costs you the effort and returns nothing. So they now
surface in the scene export and in the writing guide that sits beside the manuscript while I draft,
and the guide shows every scene card field rather than a curated few, with a minimize toggle for
when I want the screen back.

Also made the manuscript sidebar collapsible, which is a small thing that matters on a laptop.

files.name: 2026-08-14.md

frontmatter.title: The app became something I can use on a phone

files.body:
Twenty commits taking the app from desktop-only to an installable phone app, ending at v2.0.0. Six
phases: the install shell, then the layout, then the easy workspaces, then dragging, then the hard
canvases — the relation graph, the timeline, the story planner.

Two bugs worth keeping.

Dropping an event on the timeline landed it years away from where I released it. The drop was being
measured against the wrong thing, and on a phone — where the whole gesture is your thumb covering
the target — it was unusable rather than merely annoying.

The second one cost me the most and taught me the most. Any modal opened from a mobile pane was
dead: it painted perfectly and swallowed every tap. The pane marks the rest of the app inert so
touches can't leak through, and the browser then excludes that whole region from hit testing — so
the modal drawn inside it was visible and untouchable. Everything now goes through one shared modal
that escapes the pane entirely. I'd have found this in ten minutes on a device and spent an hour
looking at it in a desktop browser at phone width.

Also took the chance to fix two things I'd have defended if asked: a timing guess where a real
measurement belonged, and styles being injected at runtime into the editor.

The standing rule out of today is that mobile isn't a follow-up. If a change only works on desktop,
it's half-done.

files.name: 2026-08-15.md

frontmatter.title: What shipping to a phone actually revealed

files.body:
The biggest day so far, and it started with three bugs that only exist once something is genuinely
installed rather than merely responsive.

Signing in with Google inside the installed app bounced you straight back to the login screen. The
service worker — the thing that makes it work offline — only registered after sign-in, so a first
visit got none of it. And the page itself was being cached for an hour, which meant shipping a fix
and watching people keep the old one. None of these can be found on localhost. You have to install
the thing and use it.

Then a long stretch of making the manuscript editor feel like a manuscript editor: book typography
with a draft/page toggle, dialogue tools that do curly quotes and new-speaker line breaks properly,
export to .docx and Markdown, autocorrect, and find-and-replace.

The part I'm most glad about is less visible. I added a test harness and wrote the first real tests,
made the app degrade to local storage instead of half-dying when Firebase can't start, and fixed
backups that didn't actually contain the project — which is a terrifying sentence to write about a
feature named backup. Then I broke the largest component into pieces and deleted AI Loom outright.

Deleting AI Loom was the right call. It generated prose. I don't want an app that writes for me; I
want one that notices things about what I wrote. Everything I built afterwards — the Chekhov ledger
that pairs setups with payoffs, character arcs, the scene rhythm strip, prose diagnostics for echoed
words and filter words — follows from that. They tell me things and never touch the text.

files.name: 2026-08-16.md

frontmatter.title: Magic systems got their own category

files.body:
Two themes today: making the app easier to extend, and then immediately using that to add the thing
I'd been faking.

The extensibility work first — one registry for local-mode collections instead of the same list
copied in several places, the sprawling Analysis Hub split into per-tab panels, and form fields
described by the schema rather than hand-built one at a time. Boring, and it paid for itself within
hours.

Because then: Systems. Magic, technology, whatever set of rules your world runs on. I'd previously
handled this with four fixed fields bolted onto a scene, which was a guess about what a system is
that turned out to be wrong for every system I actually wrote. Now a system is a first-class thing
you can define, and a scene records which ones it invokes. Existing data migrates itself, once,
without asking.

I also changed how this project ships. Previously every phase got its own version and release. That
meant releasing things I hadn't looked at together, which is how you find out two features are fine
alone and contradictory side by side. Now a group of phases ends at a gate, and only gates ship.

Ended the day starting in-world calendars, so a story can have its own months and its own year
count rather than pretending everything happens in ours.

Also shipped: a global search palette, margin comments on the manuscript, and writing history with
targets.

files.name: 2026-08-17.md

frontmatter.title: Fifty-four commits, and one feature deleted

files.body:
The longest day on this project. Four release gates, v2.11.0 through v2.15.0.

The Continuity Audit landed, with four checks that know when to shut up — a check that fires on every
scene gets ignored, so each one has conditions under which it stays quiet. Alongside it, dual
ordering, so the Storyboard reads in either narrative or chronological order.

Then progressions: how an entity changes over time, with a resolver to ask what something looked like
at a given point, and a stated rule for mixed indexing. That made the dead-character-speaking check
possible, which is exactly the kind of error you don't catch by rereading.

More in the same day — typed relationships and four layout modes for the Relation Graph, nested maps
and layers on the Lore Maps canvas, custom fields per lore category, three new categories, entity
templates, an unwritten-entity worklist, unlinked mentions, location mood boards, EPUB export,
read-aloud, chapter word-count targets, accessibility controls, Markdown and .docx import, and
project-wide restore checkpoints built on word-level snapshot diffs.

Two things I'd point at rather than the volume.

I ran a fix wave — a deliberate pass through review findings, rather than fixing things as I tripped
over them. The critical one: code was setting a key to undefined instead of omitting it, which
Firestore treats very differently from the local mock.

And I deleted Lore Maps entirely, three commits after building more of it that same day. Code, docs
and stray references. It was a feature I wanted rather than one the app needed, and keeping it would
have meant maintaining a second canvas forever. Also deleted the Character Dashboard, folding it into
Lore Explorer so there's one character editor instead of two that drift apart.

files.name: 2026-08-18.md

frontmatter.title: Letting someone read the book without an account

files.body:
Two gates, v2.16.0 and v2.17.0. The first was sharing, which is the first feature in this app that
lets anyone other than me see anything.

That made it the first feature where being wrong is expensive. A share link opens a read-only view
with no account required, so everything about it had to be built assuming the reader is a stranger:
a separate, deliberately narrow set of rules for what public data can be touched, and a sanitiser
that strips anything not meant to leave. It refuses links whose destination it can't vouch for
rather than passing them through, and I proved the rules against a local emulator instead of
trusting that they read correctly. Readers can leave feedback, which lands in the same worklist as
my own margin comments — one place to look, not two.

Alongside it, series support: several books sharing one codex of characters and places, so an entity
can belong to the series rather than to a single book. A share can then cover one book or the whole
series.

The second gate was help. The app had grown far more fields than anyone could guess the meaning of,
including me on a bad day. Rather than write help text twice, the in-app help is generated from the
reference document I already maintain, so there's no second copy to drift. Every field can carry a
small "?" that explains itself in place.

Also settled that the name is Worldbuilder, one word, everywhere. It had been spelled three ways.

files.name: 2026-08-19.md

frontmatter.title: The bug that hid every piece of feedback

files.body:
Wrote help text and proper labels for the fields across every category, which is unglamorous and was
overdue — a form full of terms only I understand is a form only I can fill in.

Then a density pass on mobile. The phone layout had been a direct translation of the desktop one,
which meant enormous headings, padding sized for a mouse, and about a third of the screen doing
nothing. Tighter type, edge-to-edge panes, denser lists.

The bug of the day was the worst kind. Reader feedback on a shared link was arriving and being stored
correctly, and the worklist showed nothing at all. Not an error, not an empty state that admitted
uncertainty — just a clean, confident "no feedback". The query needed an index that didn't exist, so
it failed quietly and the screen reported the failure as an answer. Anyone who'd left me notes on the
manuscript would have assumed I'd read them and ignored them.

That's the shape of failure I keep meeting on this project: something breaks and the interface fills
the gap with a plausible-looking nothing. A visible error is always better.

Also made local mode reject the same bad writes that the real database rejects. They'd been diverging,
which meant testing locally could pass while the live version quietly refused — the exact thing local
mode exists to prevent.

Two follow-up fixes after that: mobile layers opening behind the sheet that spawned them, and a
calendar day field that would run away from you as you typed.

files.name: 2026-08-20.md

frontmatter.title: Nobody should have to paste a UUID

files.body:
Two releases, both fixing places where the app made me do its work for it.

The first was dates. Entering an in-world date meant typing numbers into boxes, which is slow and
wrong often enough to be irritating. Now you tap a calendar and a clock, in your own world's months.
Scenes can also carry a date relative to another scene — "three days after the funeral" — because
that's how I actually think about chronology while drafting. Absolute dates come later, if ever.

The second was worse and had been there a long time. Linking one entity to another meant pasting its
unique id, a string of random characters, into a field. I'd built it that way early on because it was
easy to build, and then I got used to it — which is the part that bothers me. I stopped noticing that
the app was asking me to look up an internal identifier and copy it by hand. You now type the name.

Both are the same lesson from different angles: the app should meet me where I'm thinking. If I'm
thinking about a funeral three days ago, or about a character named Elias, that's what I should be
able to type.

files.name: 2026-08-23.md

frontmatter.title: Fields that link instead of describing

files.body:
Four releases, all about the same complaint: the app kept asking me to write out things it already
knew.

Eight fields that had been free text — the sort of thing where you type a character's name into a
box about another character — now link to the actual entity. Once they link, the connection works in
both directions and shows up everywhere that entity appears, instead of being a name I typed that
happens to match. The version where you describe a relationship in prose looks equivalent and gives
you nothing back.

Also: a Reference Panel that keeps the same shape whichever entity you open, rather than rearranging
itself depending on which fields happen to be filled. That instability made it useless for glancing
at, which is its entire job. And a Lore Explorer that finally uses the width of a desktop screen
instead of one narrow column with acres of grey either side.

One fix I'd call an admission rather than a bug. The Storyboard's opening field was labelled Goal,
and I'd been filling it with a description of the scene every single time. Rather than train myself,
I relabelled it to what everyone was actually using it for. When the whole user base gets a field
wrong the same way, the field is wrong.

files.name: 2026-08-24.md

frontmatter.title: Killing a character became something the app knows about

files.body:
Character death, properly modelled. Until today a character dying was just something that happened in
the prose, which meant nothing downstream could know about it — the app would happily let a dead
character speak eleven chapters later and say nothing.

Now a death is pinned to the scene it happens in. Mark it from the writing guide or the storyboard,
undo it if the draft changes its mind, and there's a read-only status ledger showing who's alive, who
isn't, and where it happened. Because it's pinned to a scene rather than set as a flag, it moves
correctly when scenes get reordered, which they constantly do.

Three defects turned up in the logic before it shipped and one after — a retry could leave the record
half-written, orphaning the death from the character. Worth saying plainly: I found those by writing
tests for the reasoning before wiring any of it to a button. The alternative is discovering it in
December when a ledger tells me someone's alive who died in chapter nine.

Earlier in the day, a release making the writing guide something you open when you want it, with an
explicit End Scene, and Write Scene taking you to the scene rather than the top of the chapter.

Also pinned the mobile manuscript box above the keyboard toolbar. Typing on a phone and watching your
own sentence disappear behind the keyboard is the kind of thing that makes you close the app.

files.name: 2026-08-25.md

frontmatter.title: Stopped losing edits I had not saved

files.body:
Nine commits, two releases, v2.28.0 and v2.29.0.

The whole day was one theme: the app was throwing away work. Switching tabs or chapters discarded
pending manuscript edits. Leaving the Lore Explorer with unsaved changes lost them silently.

Fixed both. Added a dirty-tracking layer to the lore form with an "Unsaved changes" pill, and made
leaving park the edits rather than drop them — you get them back when you return, instead of a dialog
asking whether you meant it. Cross-workspace history plumbing so navigation between workspaces is a
real route with real entries.

Losing someone's writing is the worst thing a writing app can do. Everything else is an
inconvenience; that one makes you stop trusting it, and you don't come back.

Also fixed the Reference Panel's Physical Description and Voice fields and its prose truncation,
added an Edit-in-Lore jump from the panel, and put the Writing Scene Guide on the mobile keyboard
toolbar.

files.name: 2026-09-02.md

frontmatter.title: The Chekhov ledger stopped guessing

files.body:
A gate about making the analysis tools stop pretending to be more certain than they are.

The Chekhov ledger pairs setups with payoffs — the gun on the wall in chapter one, fired in chapter
twelve. It had been inferring those pairs, which works until two setups look similar and it
confidently pairs the wrong ones. Now a payoff can name the exact setup it settles, picked from a
list, and the panel says which pairings I stated and which it guessed. It also reports them in the
order they appear in the book rather than the order it happened to process them, which sounds trivial
and was the difference between a useful list and a scrambled one.

Same principle in the continuity audit. It was flagging events as impossibly close together using
scenes that had no time of day recorded at all — inventing precision from missing data. It now grades
findings by how much it actually knows, and where several scenes conflict it reports the worst one
rather than the first one it stumbled into.

Also redrew the character arc as a real chart instead of an approximation, then immediately fixed it
distorting its own dots and labels when the container changed size.

Smaller things: the deaths section in the scene modal collapses, and you can carry the previous
scene's cast forward with one click instead of re-tagging six people who never left the room.

files.name: 2026-09-03.md

frontmatter.title: Dialogue attribution stopped counting names

files.body:
Two things today, and both were replacing a cheap approximation with something that actually reasons.

Magic systems got costs. A system can define a reserve — mana, stamina, whatever it is in your world
— and each time a scene invokes it, it says who used it and how much it drained. That produces a
track per character showing their reserve rising and falling through the book, and a check that fires
when someone spends more than they have. The rule I stuck to: it reports the recovery that actually
happened in the text, not the amount they theoretically should have regained. Where it had to infer
who was wielding something from whose viewpoint the scene is in, it marks that point as inferred
rather than quietly presenting a guess as a fact.

I also removed the tier escalation ladder I'd built earlier the same day. It imposed a structure on
magic systems that only suited the one I had in mind.

The second half: dialogue attribution. Working out who said a line had been done by seeing whose name
appeared nearby, which is barely better than a coin flip in a scene with three people in it. Replaced
with a cascade of real rules, tried in order of confidence. Everything downstream that claims to know
who's speaking now rests on that instead.

Then the beginning of bring-your-own-key AI support, so the rules engine can hand its genuinely
ambiguous lines to a model. Mostly a day of finding out which providers can be called from a browser
at all, and making failures say what actually went wrong instead of guessing from a status code.

files.name: 2026-09-04.md

frontmatter.title: AI that labels, never writes

files.body:
Shipped the AI work and wrote down the constraint that governs it: the model labels things, it never
generates prose. It gets the lines the rules engine honestly can't attribute and returns a name. It
never writes a sentence that ends up in my book, and it never returns a number I then present as a
measurement.

I recorded that as a standing rule rather than leaving it as an intention, because it's the sort of
thing that erodes one reasonable-sounding feature at a time. I deleted an AI prose feature back in
August for exactly this reason and I'd rather not relearn it.

Several releases across the day, and most of them were the same lesson: a failing run has to say what
failed. Early on it would report a generic error while the provider had sent a perfectly clear
explanation. A rate limit now reads as "not yet" rather than "broken", since those need completely
different responses from me. And you choose which chapters to run rather than paying for the whole
manuscript to answer a question about chapter three.

The other half of the day was analysis that needed the better attribution to be possible at all:
checking whether a character's dialogue matches the idiolect I recorded for them, ranking who
actually speaks to whom, and naming setups I forgot to mark so I can mark them with a click.

Two small parsing fixes I enjoyed: it was reading contractions as quote marks, and treating a
paragraph's several quoted lines as one utterance.

Also added a daily word goal that survives having the app open in two tabs.

files.name: 2026-09-05.md

frontmatter.title: Rebuilt the plot timeline as a thread chart

files.body:
Two releases of the Story Planner and Timeline overhaul today, v2.43.0 and v2.44.0.

The first gate was mostly about admitting a feature hadn't worked. The Snowflake Wizard was meant to
walk you from a one-line premise up to a full outline, and in practice nobody finished it — you'd get
three steps in and abandon it. I pulled it out and replaced it with eleven starter Jots you can pick
up in any order, or ignore entirely.

Two follow-ups from that, both small and both my own fault:

- The starter Jots inherited copy from the wizard that promised automation they don't do. Writing a
  cheque the feature can't cash is worse than saying nothing.
- "Add Starter Jots" was confirming through a dialog whose primary button was a red *Delete*. It had
  been that way for a while, which is the part that bothers me — I'd looked straight past it more
  than once.

The second gate was the interesting one. Plot threads can now branch and merge, which meant the
timeline could no longer be drawn as a set of parallel lines. Redrew it as a proper thread chart
where a branch visibly leaves its parent and a merge visibly rejoins.

That surfaced a real bug rather than a cosmetic one. The code that works out the shape could be
handed a cycle — threads that eventually loop back into each other — and the cycle-breaking picked an
essentially arbitrary edge to cut, so the same project could render a different shape between runs.
Now it demotes the thread that closes the ring specifically, which is both stable and the answer a
reader would expect.

Non-determinism in a rendering path is the kind of bug that wastes a whole afternoon later,
because you can't reproduce it on demand. Worth the detour.

files.name: 2026-09-06.md

frontmatter.title: Jots stopped belonging to the account

files.body:
Finished moving Jots — the loose-notes workspace — from living on your account to living inside a
project, and cleaned up the bug that move exposed.

The bug: switching projects silently threw away whatever you typed next. The workspace would keep
showing the old project's note under the new project's name, and your next keystroke got saved to
an address that no longer existed. In one mode that write is quietly discarded, in the other it's
rejected. Either way the writing is gone and nothing tells you. That's the worst class of bug this
app can have, so the rule for what should be selected after a switch came out of the workspace and
into its own tested piece — it has a trap in it, two projects can coincidentally hold notes with
the same id, and the old code trusted that.

Then the migration for anyone who already had notes from before the move: ask once, pick which
project the old notes belong to, move them in, done.

Two smaller things I'd been walking past. Creating a project dropped you on an empty workspace — a
blank page is a question the app should answer, not ask, so new projects now arrive with starter
notes and the Read Me open. And the "Add Starter Jots" button was clickable when there was no
project to add them to.

Also set up this log. From here every session writes the day's entry as the work happens rather
than at the end, and the rules live in the repo so I don't have to keep repeating them. I'd asked
for the folder to be called `logs`; the format contract says `log`. The contract wins.

## Later — finishing it

Notes now travel with a project's backup. Leaving them out was right while they belonged to the
account, and wrong the moment they didn't — a backup that quietly drops every note in a project
isn't a backup.

Then the thing I only found by opening the migration screen myself instead of trusting the report
on it, and it's the same shape as the switch bug: a failure hiding behind a success message. If a
note failed to move it was skipped, the migration marked itself finished anyway, and that note was
stranded with the prompt never coming back. The likely cause is a note too long for the database to
swallow in one piece — exactly the kind of note I write. It now refuses to finish unless every note
lands, and says which didn't.

I checked all this in a browser before shipping, but against a fake account rather than my own. The
migration asks once which project your old notes belong to, and running it for real would have
answered that question for me. Not my call to make.

Shipped as v2.46.0.

Cut v2.46.1 straight after, with nothing in it. Two sessions had been committing to this repo at
once today and I wanted certainty rather than a reassurance that neither had left work stranded.
Checking said everything was already pushed and the only commits after the release were log entries,
so the running app was current either way — but "I checked and it's fine" is worth less than a tag
you can point at. An empty release is a cheap way to buy that.


## Later still — the chapter kept jumping to the top

Writing on the phone had a habit that finally annoyed me enough to chase: leave the app for
under a minute, come back, and the chapter you were in the middle of was scrolled back to its
first line. Your cursor was still exactly where you left it — tap once and you're typing in the
right place — but you had to scroll a thousand words to see what you were typing.

It turned out not to be about backgrounding at all. When the keyboard comes up, the prose box
stops being an ordinary block on the page and becomes its own little scrolling window, pinned
between the header and the toolbar so the writing area gets its height back on a small screen.
That swap is deliberate and I like it. What nobody had thought about is that a scrolling box
that has just come into existence starts at the top, and nothing ever moved it. Every keyboard
down-and-up did it; backgrounding was just the easiest way to trigger one. The reverse was
broken too — put the keyboard away and the page underneath was near the top, because the box
had been covering it and nobody was watching where it sat.

The fix is to notice which thing is doing the scrolling right now and put the cursor back about
a third of the way down it, in both directions. A third rather than the middle because it leaves
the paragraphs you just wrote on screen, which is the context you actually want.

The awkward part is that the box keeps growing while the keyboard slides in, so one correction
gets measured against a box that isn't finished yet — it has to keep re-checking until the size
holds still. And it has to know when to get out of the way: the moment you scroll it yourself,
put a finger on it, or type a character, it stops. A helpful nudge that fights you is worse than
no nudge.

That fixed the case where the app was still running. It doesn't help when the phone actually
kills it, or the tab reloads, or you come back the next morning — then the cursor is genuinely
gone and the chapter opens at the top with nothing to put back. So the position is now written
down, per device, and restored when you reopen the chapter. Four hundred milliseconds after the
cursor settles, and immediately whenever you leave: switching chapters, tapping out of the prose,
or the phone shoving the app into the background, which on a phone is usually the last thing that
happens before it gets killed.

I decided against syncing this to the account. It would mean a write on every sentence, and where
you stopped on your phone is rarely where you want to resume on a laptop — it's a device habit,
not a fact about the manuscript. Fifty chapters are remembered, oldest forgotten first, and the
whole thing is treated as untrusted on the way back in: it's storage a user can edit and it
outlives deploys, so a garbled entry has to be a shrug rather than a crash. A position past the
end of a chapter that's since been trimmed lands at the end.

It places the cursor and stops there — it doesn't open the keyboard. iOS won't do that without a
tap anyway, and an app that starts typing at you before you've asked is obnoxious on a laptop too.

Two things I got wrong in the first pass and only saw while wiring this up. The correction knew to
stand down when you typed, but not when something else moved the cursor — so a jump to a scene or
a search result would land, and then half a second later the earlier correction would drag the
view back to where the cursor used to be. And the cleanup on leaving the workspace was starting a
correction nobody would ever stop; harmless in practice because it times out, but it worked by
accident rather than on purpose. Both now say what they mean.

Checked both halves in a browser at a phone width before shipping: with the cursor left in the
middle of a long chapter, closing and reopening the keyboard now lands it a third of the way down
the box instead of at the top, and after a hard reload the chapter reopens exactly where it was —
with the cursor waiting there rather than the keyboard springing up. Shipped as v2.47.0.

## Killing the health strip

Deleted the row of count chips across the top of the Analysis Hub. It had ten tabs' worth of
numbers in it — unpaid plants, continuity errors, uncosted invocations — each one clicking through
to the tab that explains it.

I built it because ten tabs with no landing surface felt unfriendly: nothing told you what needed
attention without visiting each tab and already knowing what it was for. That reasoning was fine
and the thing I built to satisfy it was still wrong, because the Hub already has a landing surface.
It's called Overview and it's the first tab. So the strip was a second front door in front of the
first one, and it charged rent: it sat above the tab row on *every* tab, so a chunk of vertical
space went to duplicate numbers no matter which one you were reading. On a phone that's most of
what you can see at once. Every count it showed is still computed and still displayed by the tab
that owns it, so removing it loses nothing except the copy.

What made it interesting is what fell out. The Hub's tab row is icon-only below 768px, and I'd
justified that at the time by pointing at the chips right above it — the labels are there, just one
row up. Which means the strip I was about to delete was the only thing telling a phone user what
those ten icons were. Ten unlabelled icons is not a navigation bar, it's a puzzle.

So the tabs got their labels back at every width. They can't share the row equally anymore now that
they have text in them, so the row scrolls sideways instead — which is exactly what the chip row
did, so the gesture is one a user of this screen already had. Desktop is untouched.

Small lesson I keep relearning: a feature that's quietly propping up another one won't announce
itself. You find out when you pull it.

Checking the scrolling row in a browser turned up the thing I hadn't thought about: which tab you're
on is remembered globally, but where the row is scrolled to isn't. Leave the Hub on one of the last
tabs, come back, and the row is back at the start with the highlight sitting off-screen — so the
screen reads as having nothing selected. That's worse on a phone but it isn't a phone bug; a 1440px
window overflows too. The row now scrolls the selected tab into view on arrival and on every change,
at every width.

One more thing the release check caught, and it's the failure shape I keep finding: something
half-landing with nothing to announce it. The write-up of this change went into the reference doc
but never made it into the Help panel inside the app, because the compiled copy had been mistaken
for leftover clutter in the working folder and left behind. Nothing errors when that happens —
the doc is right, the app quietly says something older. My own build had muddied the water enough
to make the mistake reasonable, which is the part worth remembering: the check is to look at the
file, not to work out whose it was.

Shipped as v2.48.0.

files.name: 2026-09-08.md

frontmatter.title: The day I stopped guessing at Google

files.body:
I want to point the app at my Google Docs and have them turn up as notes, kept in step as I edit
them. There's a plan for it that runs to six phases, and all six rested on assumptions nobody had
checked. Two sittings today, both spent replacing a guess with a measurement.

The first assumption was about permissions. Google's cheap permission level is per-file — you get
what the user hands you through the picker and nothing more. What isn't documented is what happens
when the thing handed over is a *folder*. Does that reach the files inside, or just the folder? The
permission level that would settle it outright needs a formal security assessment, which is absurd
for a personal app. So I built the smallest possible thing that answers the question and nothing
else.

The answer is no. Picking a folder grants you the folder and its contents stay invisible. Asking
for them doesn't even fail — you get a perfectly cheerful empty list, which is the worst way to be
told no. Two false starts before I could trust that, both mine: the screen first reported success
on an empty result because I'd written the check to treat "no error" as "it worked", and then the
pick wasn't registering at all because I'd left out a parameter the picker needs to record the
grant, having read it as optional. For about an hour I had an answer that looked much worse than
the truth. Rather than take the failure at face value I tested the fallback in the same sitting:
picking documents individually works, and the permission grows by exactly what you picked. The
feature survives, one shape smaller — you choose documents rather than a folder, and adding one
later is a deliberate act rather than something that happens by itself.

The second sitting was the piece that turns a Google Doc into a note, and the same lesson landed
again. I had already guessed twice at what a Docs export looks like and been wrong both times, so
this time I exported a real chapter and read it. Three things in there would have quietly wrecked
my research. Most of the formatting markers say *nothing is applied here* — 29 of 41 — so a
converter that emphasises anything carrying a marker bolds the entire document. Runs of text split
mid-word, so joining them with a space sprinkles "two w eeks" through prose nobody re-reads line by
line. And every link is wrapped in a Google tracking redirect, so unprocessed, each cited source
points back at Google with a timestamp attached. Tables can't survive at all — the editor has no
notion of one — so each row becomes a line with the cells separated by pipes: content kept, grid
honestly lost.

The rest is rules about what a sync may do. It never overwrites a note I've edited, never deletes
one because a file went missing, and never fetches a document that hasn't changed. There's a
version stamp folded into the fingerprints so improving the converter later re-does the notes
instead of declaring every one of them conflicted forever.

Also found the throwaway test screen was unreachable but still being shipped, keys and all — the
bundler doesn't drop code just because nothing can reach it. Unreachable and absent aren't the same
thing.

files.name: 2026-09-09.md

frontmatter.title: The whole Drive feature, and three ways it could have eaten my prose

files.body:
Seven sittings and two releases, and the thing I set out to build a couple of days ago is done: my
research in Google Drive turns up in the app as notes and keeps itself current, a note that's
changed on both sides hands me the decision instead of picking for me, and any file on this machine
can become a note without Google being involved at all.

The only test I actually cared about all day was one I ran by hand. Edit a note here, edit the same
document in Drive, sync. If the app had quietly taken Drive's version, the whole feature would have
been a liability dressed up as a convenience. It stopped, said the note had been edited in both
places, and left my words alone.

Which is the theme of the day, really. Almost everything hard was a way this could have destroyed
something without ever telling me, and three of them nearly shipped. The sync works out that I've
deleted a note by not finding it in the list it was handed — perfectly correct until the list hasn't
loaded yet, at which point every mirrored document looks deleted and stops syncing for good,
silently. The background permission check was set to an option I was sure meant "don't show
anything", and it actually means "skip the consent screen if they've already agreed" — so the app
would have thrown a Google popup at me roughly hourly, unprompted. And the worst one arrived through
the button built to prevent exactly this: pressing "keep mine" has to convince the next sync there's
nothing left to do, but there are *two* separate reasons it can decide a note needs rewriting, and
clearing one and not the other makes the button look like it worked and then overwrites the words I
just chose to keep, five minutes later, with nothing on screen. There's a test now that starts in
that state and insists the next sync does nothing at all.

None of those would have failed loudly. That's what makes them worth the paranoia — a crash you find
in a minute; a note quietly replaced overnight you find in a month, if ever. The same instinct runs
through the rest of it: the access token is never written down anywhere, none of the Drive
bookkeeping goes into a backup, and keeping my own version asks Google when the document actually
changed rather than guessing, refusing to resolve at all if it can't reach it.

The smaller feature took an hour because the hard part already existed. Point at a Markdown file, a
Word document or a saved web page and it becomes a note, formatting intact, no account and no
network needed. One rule in there is invisible and would produce garbage backwards: Markdown has to
become markup *before* the sanitiser sees it, or every heading and bullet collapses into one grey
slab that looks almost right until you read it. I'd learned that on the Drive side already, so this
time there's a test that fails the moment anyone removes the step. An imported note is deliberately
just a note — no pretend link back to a file nothing is watching.

Two things about writing it all down. Documenting a feature forces you to notice what it doesn't do,
and three honest limitations went into the docs that I'd been comfortably not saying out loud — then
a day later two of them stopped being true and I had to go back and fix a limitations list that was
now *underselling* the thing, which is exactly as untrustworthy as one that oversells it. And I'd
been filing each sitting as its own dated file, so one day had four. That's not a daily log, that's
four fragments of a Tuesday. Merged them and changed the rules so it doesn't happen again; the
format always allowed either shape, so this was my own habit drifting rather than a spec problem.

Left undone on purpose: it only syncs while I'm actually looking at my notes, and nothing syncs with
the app closed. There's no server to receive Google's nudge, and there isn't going to be one.
